paragraphs: Automatic differentiation computes derivatives by following the operations in a program. This paper asks how that practical procedure relates to mathematical differentiation when the function being computed is nonsmooth. The distinction matters because a program's derivative calculations need a sound interpretation if they are to support an analysis of learning algorithms.

The authors develop a mathematical framework consisting of a class of functions and a calculus for handling their nonsmooth behavior. They connect this framework to stochastic approximation methods, bringing program differentiation and the analysis of iterative learning into the same account. The contribution is therefore a way to reason about computations already used in machine learning.

A central finding concerns artificial critical points created by algorithmic differentiation: points that appear critical because of the differentiation procedure. The paper identifies this issue and shows that the usual methods covered by its analysis avoid those points with probability one. This connects a potential mathematical complication to its consequences for stochastic learning, rather than simply treating every computed derivative as an ordinary smooth derivative.
neurips-2020-a-mathematical-model-for-au.tldr: The paper provides a nonsmooth mathematical framework for automatic differentiation and explains why usual learning methods almost surely avoid the artificial critical points it can create.

paragraphs: The problem is to select an option whose average reward is within ε of the best available option, with confidence at least 1−δ. Each option is an arm that must be sampled to learn about its reward. The paper studies how many samples this task requires in the worst case, with particular attention to precise leading constants.

The authors introduce an elimination approach whose sample complexity approaches n/(2ε²) times log(1/δ) as the number of arms n grows, provided δ is at least 1/n. This matches the stated optimal sample complexity for learning the means of the n arms separately. They also establish a conditional matching lower bound for the broad class of elimination algorithms.

When n is independent of δ, their approach instead approaches 2n/ε² times log(1/δ). The abstract reports improvements exceeding factors of 1500, and 6000 in the δ≥1/n regime, over the best previously known algorithm. These are sample-complexity comparisons. The result sharpens what elimination can achieve, while its optimality claim retains the stated algorithm-class and parameter conditions.
neurips-2020-an-optimal-elimination-algo.tldr: A new elimination method identifies an approximately best arm with asymptotically sharp sample complexity under stated confidence conditions.

paragraphs: A variational autoencoder must balance reconstructing its examples against learning latent representations that generalize. This paper studies how to control that balance through the divergence used to regularize the latent space. Its setting reconstructs an example through a latent representation whose dimension is no larger than the original input dimension.

The authors propose regularization based on a skew-geometric Jensen–Shannon divergence. By examining limiting cases, they develop a variant that interpolates between forward and reverse KL divergence. The interpolation applies both to distributions and to divergences, giving the skew parameter a direct interpretation in latent space. Low-dimensional examples illustrate why this flexibility could help a VAE.

The paper then evaluates the approach quantitatively and qualitatively. In the reported experiments, adjusting the skew of the proposed variant improves reconstruction and generation relative to several baseline VAEs. The method is entirely unsupervised and uses one interpretable hyperparameter. The findings support divergence choice as a useful way to shape latent-space regularization, with the improvement demonstrated in the experiments described rather than established for every VAE.
neurips-2020-constraining-variational-in.tldr: An adjustable geometric Jensen–Shannon regularizer improves reconstruction and generation over several VAE baselines in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns labels throughout an image, but adaptation becomes difficult when target images come from mixed conditions or previously unseen domains. This paper studies that open compound setting. It moves beyond the single-source, single-target setup emphasized by earlier work and organizes adaptation around the different domains hidden within the target collection.

The method has three stages. First, it groups target images by style to discover latent domains. Next, image translation creates corresponding versions of source images, effectively synthesizing source-side counterparts for those target domains. Finally, it learns target-to-source alignment separately for the paired domains. This pairing gives each adaptation problem a more specific source and target.

The main idea is to turn one complicated adaptation problem into several simpler unsupervised adaptation problems. Style discovery establishes the groups, image translation establishes their counterparts, and separate alignment connects them. On the GTA-to-C-driving benchmark, the authors report a new state-of-the-art result. That finding supports the proposed decomposition for the evaluated setting, where treating all target data as one uniform domain would overlook its internal variation.
neurips-2020-discover-hallucinate-and-ad.tldr: The method adapts semantic segmentation to mixed target domains by discovering styles, synthesizing matching source domains, and aligning each pair separately.

paragraphs: Constrained optimization can be expensive when each update requires projecting a point back into a complicated feasible set. Projection-free methods avoid that operation, which can make individual iterations more efficient. This paper develops such methods for saddle point problems that are convex in one variable and strongly concave in the other.

The proposed algorithm combines Conditional Gradient Sliding with Mirror-Prox. In the batch setting, its stated requirements are approximately 1/√ε gradient evaluations and 1/ε² linear optimizations, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Reporting these separately matters: the method controls the number of gradient calculations while using linear optimization to handle the constraints without projection.

The authors also extend the approach to stochastic optimization and present what they describe as the first stochastic projection-free algorithms for saddle point problems. Their experiments demonstrate effectiveness and support the theoretical guarantees. Together, the results provide an approach for the specified convex–strongly-concave setting that makes the computational roles of gradients and constraint handling explicit, especially when the geometry of the constraints makes projection inconvenient.
neurips-2020-efficient-projection-free-a.tldr: Combining Conditional Gradient Sliding with Mirror-Prox yields projection-free saddle point algorithms with theoretical guarantees in batch and stochastic settings.

paragraphs: Analyses of neural activity often assume that an environment has one stable population representation. This paper addresses situations in which that assumption misses important variation. A population may represent the same environment differently across trials, and ambiguous cues may cause it to switch rapidly between representations during a single trial.

The authors develop a state-space framework with two complementary components. An observation model permits multiple activity patterns for the same stimulus or environment. A state model describes the moment-by-moment probability that the representation changes. Together, these components produce instantaneous estimates of which stimulus or environment the population currently represents, while allowing both variable firing patterns and changing represented content.

The framework is applied to activity in the CA1 region of a mouse's hippocampus during movement through ambiguous virtual environments. The analysis finds substantial trial-to-trial representational variation in many cells. It also finds that population representations can switch rapidly between environments within a trial when spatial cues are most ambiguous. These findings show why a model that permits both variability and rapid switching can reveal structure obscured by a single stable representation.
neurips-2020-estimating-fluctuations-in-.tldr: A state-space model reveals variable and rapidly switching hippocampal representations in a mouse navigating ambiguous virtual environments.

paragraphs: Paid prediction APIs differ in both price and performance, and their strengths can vary across a user's data. FrugalML addresses the resulting decision problem: how to choose an API, or a sequence of APIs, while respecting a budget. Its starting point is that the best service to use need not be the same for every example.

The framework learns where each API performs well or poorly and optimizes an adaptive sequential strategy for using the available services. It therefore treats service selection and budget allocation as a joint learning problem. The theoretical analysis identifies sparsity in the formulation that can be used to make the optimization efficient.

The experiments cover facial emotion recognition, sentiment analysis, and speech recognition using APIs from several providers. Across the evaluated tasks, FrugalML achieves up to 90% lower cost while matching the best single API's accuracy, or up to 5% better accuracy at the best API's cost. These are separate reported tradeoffs and maxima across tasks. They demonstrate that combining services according to their strengths can improve the cost–accuracy balance.
neurips-2020-frugalml-how-to-use-ml-pred.tldr: FrugalML learns budget-aware sequences of prediction APIs, achieving substantial cost savings or accuracy gains in the reported tasks.

paragraphs: Backpropagation is effective for training artificial networks, but some of its operations are biologically implausible. Target propagation offers an alternative: a top-down model turns output error into desired activity levels for individual units. Those local targets then guide weight updates. This paper asks when such updates can correspond exactly to backpropagation.

The authors derive GAIT-prop, a modified target-propagation rule in which each target is a small perturbation of the activity produced by the forward pass. They establish an exact correspondence with backpropagation under a specific condition: the synaptic weight matrices must be orthogonal. This gives the proposed rule a mathematical connection to backpropagation beyond a heuristic resemblance.

The experiments use simple computer vision tasks and a soft regularizer that encourages orthogonality. Under that setup, GAIT-prop and backpropagation show nearly identical performance. The theoretical and empirical claims are distinct: exact update equality is proved for orthogonal weights, while similar task performance is observed with a regularizer encouraging that structure. The contribution connects a biologically motivated learning mechanism to a well-established training rule under an explicit structural condition.
neurips-2020-gait-prop-a-biologically-pl.tldr: GAIT-prop exactly matches backpropagation updates with orthogonal weights and achieves nearly identical performance in simple vision experiments using an orthogonality regularizer.

paragraphs: Causal experiments are often conducted in one environment with the aim of informing decisions elsewhere. Transportability asks when knowledge can be transferred despite differences between environments. This paper extends that question beyond atomic interventions to more complex, potentially stochastic interventions, referred to as soft interventions.

The extension applies both to the interventions represented in the available information and to the target distribution being analyzed. The authors derive a graphical condition that is necessary and sufficient for soft-transportability. Within the framework, the condition therefore characterizes both when transfer is possible and when it is not, rather than supplying only a sufficient test.

They also develop an algorithm for deciding whether the effect of a non-atomic intervention can be computed from distributions available across domains. As a consequence, they establish completeness of the σ-calculus for soft-transportability. This means that the calculus is adequate for the full transfer task characterized by their theory. The contribution provides a formal basis for combining causal information across environments when interventions are more flexible than setting a variable to a fixed value.
neurips-2020-general-transportability-of.tldr: The paper gives a necessary-and-sufficient graphical criterion and a complete algorithmic framework for transporting soft-intervention effects across environments.

paragraphs: Leverage score sampling is a technique used to accelerate a range of computational problems, including kernel methods. This paper extends earlier kernel results to a broader family of kernels and connects the sampling technique to neural network theory. Its focus is the relationship between how a network is initialized and the kernel behavior associated with that initialization.

The first connection links neural network initialization to approximating the neural tangent kernel using random features. This reframes initialization as part of a kernel-approximation problem. It allows the authors to place classical random Gaussian initialization and leverage score sampling within a shared theoretical discussion, rather than treating them as unrelated ways to start training.

The second result proves an equivalence between regularized neural networks and neural tangent kernel ridge regression under both initialization schemes. That equivalence provides a bridge from a sampling method developed for computational linear algebra and kernels to an analysis of neural networks. The stated contribution is theoretical: it broadens kernel sampling results and establishes relationships between initialization, random features, and regularized learning.
neurips-2020-generalized-leverage-score-.tldr: The paper extends leverage score sampling to broader kernels and links neural network initialization and regularization to neural tangent kernel approximation and regression.

paragraphs: How can researchers recover the perceptual patterns behind judgments such as a chord's pleasantness or a face's seriousness? Existing Markov Chain Monte Carlo with People methods use repeated binary choices. The paper argues that these trials provide relatively little information and that local proposals can make exploration of the stimulus space slow.

Gibbs Sampling with People replaces binary choice with a slider that lets a participant continuously adjust one stimulus dimension toward a criterion. The authors formulate both approaches through utility theory and interpret the new procedure as Gibbs sampling. An aggregation parameter controls the transition step, allowing behavior to shift between sampling and deterministic optimization.

An initial study finds that the new method clearly outperforms the binary-choice approach. Further studies produce interpretable results for musical chords, vocal emotions, and faces, with validation through large-scale perceptual ratings. Final experiments use the method to navigate StyleGAN's latent space. This demonstrates a promising route toward exploring high-dimensional perceptual spaces by combining human judgments with a structured sampling procedure.
neurips-2020-gibbs-sampling-with-people-.tldr: Gibbs Sampling with People uses continuous human adjustments to explore perceptual representations more effectively than binary-choice sampling in the initial study.

paragraphs: Sparse linear bandits model sequential decisions with many available features but a sparse underlying structure. The learner must balance collecting information against choosing rewarding actions. This paper studies the unavoidable cost of that balance through regret bounds that do not depend on the ambient dimension.

For the setting it calls data-poor, the abstract specifies a horizon larger than the ambient dimension and feature vectors admitting a well-conditioned exploration distribution. Under these conditions, the authors establish a minimax lower bound with n^(2/3) dependence on the horizon n. An explore-then-commit algorithm provides a nearly matching upper bound, identifying that horizon dependence as optimal in the stated regime.

The paper also proves a dimension-free upper bound of order √n under an additional assumption about the signal magnitude of relevant features. The stronger guarantee therefore depends on extra structure. Together, the results distinguish what is possible under the basic exploration conditions from what becomes possible with a signal-strength assumption, and show why information gathering must be balanced carefully against immediate reward.
neurips-2020-high-dimensional-sparse-lin.tldr: The paper establishes nearly matching dimension-free n^(2/3) regret bounds for a stated sparse-bandit regime and a √n upper bound with an additional signal-strength assumption.

paragraphs: Approximate nearest-neighbor search must balance search speed, accuracy, and the memory needed to store its index. Compressing data can reduce memory use but hurt accuracy. Heterogeneous memory offers another option: combine a small amount of fast memory with a larger amount of slow memory, allowing billions of uncompressed points on one machine.

The difficulty is that access to slower memory can undermine query speed. HM-ANN is a graph-based similarity-search algorithm designed around both memory heterogeneity and data heterogeneity. Its purpose is to make the extra capacity useful without allowing inappropriate memory use to dominate the search process.

On BIGANN and DEEP1B, the authors report substantially better recall–latency tradeoffs than compression-based L&C and IMI+OPQ solutions, including 46% higher recall at the same latency. They also build heterogeneous-memory versions of HNSW and NSG for comparison. At billion-point scale, HM-ANN is respectively 2 and 5.8 times faster at the same accuracy. These findings show the value of designing the search algorithm around the memory system, beyond simply placing an existing index in larger memory.
neurips-2020-hm-ann-efficient-billion-po.tldr: HM-ANN uses heterogeneous memory for uncompressed billion-point search and improves measured recall–latency tradeoffs over the evaluated alternatives.

paragraphs: BERT's success in language understanding does not automatically make it straightforward to use for text generation. This paper builds a sequence-to-sequence framework using separate BERT models for the encoder and decoder. Lightweight adapters inserted between BERT layers are tuned on the task data, allowing the framework to use information from both pretrained models while avoiding catastrophic forgetting.

The generation procedure uses Mask-Predict, a parallel decoding algorithm chosen to accommodate BERT's bidirectional and conditionally independent nature. The components are designed as interchangeable units, and the framework can also be adapted to autoregressive decoding. The approach combines a particular parallel generation method with flexibility in how the overall system is assembled.

In machine translation experiments, the parallel version consistently outperforms the autoregressive baselines while halving inference latency. It obtains BLEU scores of 36.49 and 33.57 on the stated German-to-English tasks. The autoregressive adaptation reaches 30.60 and 43.56 on the stated English-to-German and English-to-French tasks, matching the level of the state-of-the-art baselines. The results support both efficient parallel generation and reuse of the adapter framework in sequential decoding.
neurips-2020-incorporating-bert-into-par.tldr: Lightweight adapters connect encoder and decoder BERT models to parallel translation, outperforming evaluated autoregressive baselines while halving inference latency.

paragraphs: People can often infer rules from a few examples and then combine those rules in new ways. Neural models can struggle with this kind of generalization when test cases differ systematically from training examples. This paper tackles the problem by making an explicit rule system the object that the model learns.

The proposed neuro-symbolic approach uses techniques from neural program synthesis to infer an entire system of rules from a small example set. Rather than mapping each input directly to an output, the model induces rules governing the observed examples. This changes the learning task from producing individual answers to discovering a structured account that can support compositional behavior.

The authors evaluate the approach in three domains: artificial instruction learning used to study human learning, the SCAN challenge datasets, and translation of number words into integers across many human languages. It outperforms neural meta-learning techniques in all three domains. These results support explicit rule synthesis as an effective approach to the tested generalization problems, connecting learning from limited examples with the ability to represent systematic combinations.
neurips-2020-learning-compositional-rule.tldr: A neuro-symbolic model learns explicit rule systems from few examples and outperforms neural meta-learning approaches in three compositional learning domains.

paragraphs: Implicit-depth networks define their output through a solution or equilibrium rather than a fixed sequence of layers. They can be memory efficient, but finding an equilibrium can be unstable, and a solution may lack an existence guarantee. This paper introduces Monotone Operator Equilibrium Networks, or monDEQ, to give that computation a firmer mathematical foundation.

The authors connect equilibrium computation to a monotone operator splitting problem, for which efficient solvers offer stable, guaranteed convergence. They then parameterize the network so that the relevant operators remain monotone, with their construction guaranteeing a unique equilibrium. The model design and solution procedure are therefore developed together.

The paper instantiates several versions and implements iterative solvers for structured linear operators, including multiscale convolutions. The resulting models substantially outperform the Neural ODE-based models in the reported comparison while also being more computationally efficient. The contribution joins an equilibrium existence guarantee with a convergent computational approach, showing how mathematical structure can support practical implicit-depth architectures.
neurips-2020-monotone-operator-equilibri.tldr: monDEQ builds implicit-depth networks with unique equilibria and stable solvers, outperforming the compared Neural ODE models in performance and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Adapting a neural network to a task often requires changing how inputs enter it or how outputs are produced. This paper studies when those changes preserve universal approximation: the ability to approximate any continuous function uniformly on compact sets. It provides general conditions on the feature and readout maps surrounding an architecture.

The results apply in several directions. For an architecture already capable of universal approximation, a binary-valued final layer yields deterministic approximation guarantees for classifiers. For input and output spaces that are Hadamard manifolds, the authors identify geometrically meaningful maps satisfying their criteria. Applications include universal deep networks between spaces of symmetric positive definite matrices and universality of hyperbolic feed-forward networks.

The framework also shows that randomizing every layer except the final two produces a universal function family with probability one. Additional conditions allow the first or last few layers to have widths equal to the input or output dimension without reducing approximation capability. These are representation guarantees tied to the stated conditions, explaining when useful architectural modifications preserve expressive power.
neurips-2020-non-euclidean-universal-app.tldr: The paper gives conditions under which input and output transformations preserve universal approximation, including applications to geometric networks, classifiers, and randomized layers.

paragraphs: This paper studies control of a linear dynamical system subject to adversarial perturbations. The controller receives only a scalar loss, and the loss function itself is unknown. That feedback restriction makes the learning problem demanding: the controller must improve its choices from the observed cost rather than from direct knowledge of how the loss depends on its decisions.

A central complication is memory. The current loss depends on past controls, so an action cannot be evaluated solely through its immediate consequences. The authors address this by developing an efficient method for bandit convex optimization with loss functions that depend on a history of decisions. This broader optimization problem captures the dependence that arises in control.

Using that approach, the paper gives an efficient algorithm with sublinear regret for both known and unknown systems. Sublinear regret means the cumulative comparison gap grows more slowly than the interaction horizon, so its per-step average diminishes. The contribution therefore combines limited-feedback control with a general method for handling memory in bandit optimization, which the authors identify as potentially useful beyond this application.
neurips-2020-non-stochastic-control-with.tldr: An efficient algorithm achieves sublinear regret for linear control with adversarial perturbations and scalar-loss feedback by handling the effects of past actions.

paragraphs: Exploration is especially difficult in multi-agent reinforcement learning when rewards are sparse. Agents may interact with an environment many times before receiving useful reward signals. This paper investigates whether sharing experience among agents can make that process more efficient, allowing learning to draw on information collected by different participants.

The proposed Shared Experience Actor-Critic algorithm, SEAC, implements this idea within an actor-critic framework. Its mechanism combines gradients from different agents, bringing their experiences together in the learning updates. Experience sharing is thus part of how the agents learn, with the aim of making useful exploration contribute beyond the agent that originally performed it.

Across the evaluated collection of sparse-reward multi-agent environments, SEAC consistently learns in fewer steps and reaches higher returns than several baselines and state-of-the-art algorithms. In some harder environments, sharing experience determines whether the task is learned at all. These findings show both faster learning and improved eventual performance in the tested settings, supporting experience sharing as a practical way to address sparse-reward exploration.
neurips-2020-shared-experience-actor-cri.tldr: SEAC combines learning gradients across agents and improves learning speed and returns in the evaluated sparse-reward environments.

paragraphs: This paper asks precisely how network depth changes the functions a ReLU network can represent efficiently. It develops dimension-free representation results under squared loss for a depth-indexed family of function classes, G_D. The analysis tracks both depth and neuron count, making the benefits of additional layers explicit.

For functions in G_D, networks with D ReLU layers achieve approximation rates that matching lower bounds show are sharp up to constants. Each class G_D is strictly contained in the next class, and increasing depth brings less smooth functions into the family. Moreover, using fewer than D layers gives a strictly worse approximation rate on G_D.

The technical insight is to exploit deep networks' ability to produce highly oscillatory functions using few activation functions. This supports the hypothesis that depth helps represent less smooth functions, with a graded result across depths rather than a single shallow-versus-deep comparison. The guarantees concern the function classes defined in the paper and their squared-loss approximation rates, providing a precise account of representational benefits within that setting.
neurips-2020-sharp-representation-theore.tldr: Sharp approximation bounds show how additional ReLU layers improve representation of increasingly less smooth function classes.

paragraphs: SURF estimates a probability distribution using a collection of polynomial pieces. The paper aims to combine statistical efficiency with a simpler computational procedure. Instead of relying on complicated optimization for each piece, it uses interpolation of empirical probabilities and then merges pieces through a divide-and-conquer process.

Its approximation guarantees address both broad applicability and misspecification. Known polynomial-approximation results imply coverage of a large class of common distributions. For polynomial degree at most eight, the stated robustness guarantee places the estimated distribution at an ℓ1 distance less than three times that of the nearest degree-matched piecewise polynomial. This compares performance with the best approximation even when the distribution does not itself belong to that family.

The algorithm uses optimal sample complexity and runs in time nearly linear in the sample count. When samples are already sorted, it can be parallelized to achieve sublinear running time. The authors also report experimental improvements over state-of-the-art algorithms. The contribution brings together simple construction, approximation robustness, and computational efficiency, with the degree restriction attached to the stated robustness bound.
neurips-2020-surf-a-simple-universal-rob.tldr: SURF learns piecewise-polynomial distribution estimates with optimal sample complexity, near-linear runtime, and a stated misspecification guarantee for degrees up to eight.

paragraphs: Natural gradient descent can accelerate learning, but computing with the full Fisher information is costly in large neural networks. Practical methods therefore approximate it. This paper asks why some approximations retain fast convergence and identifies conditions under which they match exact natural gradient descent.

The analysis considers deep networks in the infinite-width limit and uses the neural tangent kernel to study training in function space. Under the specified conditions, approximate and exact Fisher information produce identical function-space training dynamics and the same fast convergence to global minima. This perspective follows changes in the network's represented function rather than focusing only on changes in its parameters.

The results cover layer-wise block-diagonal approximations, block-tridiagonal approximations, and K-FAC. A unit-wise approximation also achieves the same fast convergence under additional assumptions. The unifying property is an isotropic gradient in function space, which the authors identify as fundamental to the shared convergence behavior. The paper therefore supplies a common theoretical explanation for several approximation strategies, with its conclusions tied to the infinite-width analysis and stated conditions.
neurips-2020-understanding-approximate-f.tldr: Under specific infinite-width conditions, several Fisher approximations preserve exact natural gradient descent's function-space dynamics and fast convergence.

paragraphs: Learning physical dynamics from images requires connecting high-dimensional visual observations to the coordinates that describe motion. This paper develops an unsupervised model that learns those coordinates together with Lagrangian dynamics. Its aim is to retain physical interpretability while supporting both prediction and control.

The model uses a coordinate-aware variational autoencoder designed for systems made of multiple rigid bodies moving in a plane. The autoencoder learns generalized coordinates, and the dynamics model simultaneously learns how those coordinates evolve. Accounting for the geometry of this class of physical systems gives the latent representation a role in describing mechanics, beyond serving as a compressed image representation.

The resulting interpretable dynamics capture physical properties such as kinetic and potential energy. The abstract states that these learned properties enable long-term prediction in image space and the construction of energy-based controllers. The contribution links visual learning to quantities useful for reasoning about and influencing motion. Its geometric design specifically addresses planar systems of multiple rigid bodies, connecting the image model's structure to the physical setting.
neurips-2020-unsupervised-learning-of-la.tldr: A coordinate-aware VAE learns interpretable Lagrangian dynamics from images of planar rigid-body systems, enabling long-term prediction and energy-based control.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a way to train a text generator by first searching for useful outputs. The framework, Text Generation by Learning from Search, begins with simulated annealing applied to a heuristic objective that roughly measures sentence quality. The search results supply material from which a conditional generative model can learn.

The learning stage also smooths noise in the search results. Search and learning can then alternate, allowing the process to bootstrap performance through repeated rounds. The two stages have complementary roles: search seeks sentences favored by the quality objective, while the generative model learns from those sentences and reduces the influence of their noise.

The authors evaluate the framework on unsupervised paraphrasing and text formalization. It significantly outperforms the unsupervised baselines in both tasks and reaches performance comparable to strong supervised methods for paraphrase generation. These results support search-generated training material as a useful basis for unsupervised generation. The supervised comparison applies specifically to paraphrasing, while the reported advantage over unsupervised alternatives covers both evaluated tasks.
neurips-2020-unsupervised-text-generatio.tldr: Alternating heuristic search with generative-model learning improves unsupervised paraphrasing and formalization, with paraphrasing performance comparable to strong supervised methods.

paragraphs: This paper develops a Bayesian model for projecting COVID-19 fatalities under different containment policies. It treats countries as distinct data points and uses policy variation across them to learn country-specific effects. The aim is to support comparisons between lockdown and reopening scenarios, including alternative policies within the same country.

The model combines two Gaussian-process layers. The lower layer uses an SEIR compartmental model as its prior mean, with parameters depending on the country and policy. The shared upper layer learns how those parameters relate to country features and policy indicators. This structure connects a mechanistic account of epidemic progression with statistical learning across countries.

The entire model is trained jointly using stochastic variational inference. This lets the mechanistic prior and data-driven components participate in one learning procedure. The authors compare projections with other models listed by the CDC and analyze multiple lockdown and reopening strategies. The stated output is a set of model-based fatality projections under alternative policy scenarios, providing a framework for examining how policy choices may change projected outcomes.
neurips-2020-when-and-how-to-lift-the-lo.tldr: A two-layer Bayesian model combines SEIR dynamics with cross-country learning to project COVID-19 fatalities under alternative containment and reopening policies.
